vignette:
# Marcus

Marcus is a sixty-three-year-old construction foreman with weathered hands and a quiet, measured way of speaking. He's been in the building trade for over forty years—the kind of man who knows how to read a blueprint, manage a crew, and solve problems on the fly. He's Samoan, with family roots on both sides of his ancestry, and he carries himself with the kind of dignity that comes from a lifetime of honest work. His wife of thirty-two years passed away from cancer five years ago. They had no children together, though he's remained close with her adult children from a previous relationship.

For the past eighteen months, Marcus had been seeing someone—a woman named Patricia who worked as a nurse at the local hospital. They'd met at a community event, and he'd felt hopeful about companionship again. Patricia was intelligent and seemed to understand him. But three months ago, something shifted. A disagreement about money turned into shouting. When Marcus tried to leave the room, Patricia grabbed his arm and pulled him back. When he tried again, she hit him—hard, across the face. He was shocked. He'd never been hit by a partner before. He apologized, thinking somehow he'd caused it, and they moved past it.

But it happened again. And again. Small arguments would escalate, and Patricia would become physically aggressive—pushing, hitting, once throwing a ceramic bowl that cut his shoulder. Each time, Marcus would withdraw further into himself, trying to avoid triggering her anger. He stopped going to his regular Friday dinners with his sister. He made excuses at work, claiming fatigue. His supervisor noticed he was making uncharacteristic mistakes on the job—miscalculating measurements, forgetting to check safety protocols that he'd followed religiously for decades.

The final incident came two months ago. Patricia was angry about something trivial—a text message from his sister. She cornered him in the kitchen and began hitting him repeatedly. Marcus, who is a large man, simply stood there and took it. He didn't fight back. He didn't even try to leave. He just stood there and absorbed the blows until she exhausted herself and left the house. That night, Marcus ended the relationship.

Since then, Marcus hasn't been the same. He's hypervigilant in ways that confuse him—he startles at sudden noises on the job site, even though he's worked in construction noise his entire life. He finds himself tensing when his sister raises her voice, even in normal conversation. He's lost weight. His sleep is fractured; he wakes at three or four in the morning with his heart racing, sometimes unsure where he is. At work, he's become withdrawn, delegating tasks he used to enjoy. His crew has noticed the change.

What troubles Marcus most is the shame. He's a man, a large man, a man who's supposed to be capable and strong. He struggles to articulate why he didn't leave sooner, why he apologized for things that weren't his fault, why he stood motionless while being struck. There's a persistent, gnawing sense that he should have handled it differently—that his response somehow reflects a fundamental failure in him. He doesn't like to be alone, but he also doesn't want to be around people. He's begun to wonder if he's broken in some irreparable way.
